title: Yolk Sac Tumors -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Yolk sac tumors (also known as endodermal sinus tumors) are malignant primitive germ cell tumors; they are histologically similar to the mesenchyma of the primitive yolk sac. Yolk sac tumors can be found in a pure form or mixed with other germ cell tumors. They are common in the pediatric age group and can be found anywhere in the body. To avoid the high morbidity and mortality associated with this condition, it must be promptly diagnosed and treated. This activity reviews the evaluation and treatment of the yolk sac tumors and highlights the role of the interprofessional team in evaluating and treating patients with this condition.

title: Yolk Sac Tumors -- Introduction
content: Yolk sac tumors (also known as primitive endodermal tumors or endodermal sinus tumors) are malignant primitive germ cell tumors. They are histologically similar to the mesenchyme of the primitive yolk sac. [1] [2] Yolk sac tumor is a type of germ cell tumor. Germ cell tumors commonly arise in the gonads but can also occur outside the gonads, where they are called extragonadal germ cell tumors. [3] The most common testicular tumor in young children under the age of 3 is a yolk sac tumor, and it is also known as infantile embryonal carcinoma. Yolk sac tumors have a good prognosis in this age group. [4] Compared to pure type in infants and young children, yolk sac tumors in adults are often found in combination with other types of germ cell tumors (eg, teratoma and embryonal carcinoma). [5] [6]

title: Yolk Sac Tumors -- Etiology
content: The cause of yolk sac tumors is essentially unknown. Some studies suggest that RUNX3 gene hypermethylation and GATA-4 overexpression may contribute to the pathogenesis of yolk sac tumors. [7] [8]

title: Yolk Sac Tumors -- Epidemiology
content: Yolk sac tumors are rare tumors that can occur in both genders and may be found in the ovary, testes, and other body parts. Yolk sac tumors are commonly observed in young children.

title: Yolk Sac Tumors -- Epidemiology -- Yolk Sac Tumors in Males
content: Yolk sac tumors of the testis have a bimodal age distribution, with young children under the age of 3 and post-pubertal adults. [9] In children, the yolk sac tumor is the most common testicular neoplasm. It accounts for about 30% of germ cell tumors in this age group, with a median age at diagnosis of 18 months. Usually, children have pure yolk sac tumors, and their prognosis is good. In adults, yolk sac tumors typically present as mixed germ cell tumors and present in the 2nd to 3rd decades of life. [4] [10]

title: Yolk Sac Tumors -- Epidemiology -- Yolk Sac Tumors in Females
content: Yolk sac tumors are uncommon neoplasms of the ovary, accounting for 15% of all ovarian germ cell tumors; they present in early life and rarely after age 40. The median age of diagnosis is 19 years, and 40% of patients are diagnosed in the prepubertal period. About 60% of ovarian yolk sac tumors present in a pure form, while 40% present with mixed germ cell tumors. [11]

title: Yolk Sac Tumors -- Histopathology
content: On gross examination, yolk sac tumors are soft, solid masses that are tan to yellow or grey, with a mucoid appearance; notable necrosis, cystic changes, and hemorrhage are commonly present. [12] On microscopic examination, the tumors consist of primitive tumor cells and exhibit a wide range of histological types, including microcystic/reticular, papillary, solid, festoon, polyvesicular-vitelline, glandular, intestinal, endometroid, parietal, tubular, and hepatoid. The reticular microcystic pattern is the most common type formed by vacuolated cytoplasm of tumor cells; it appears like a honeycomb under a microscope. [13] The Schiller-Duval body is pathognomonic of yolk sac tumors and appears as a glomerulus with a fibrovascular core. However, Schiller-Duvall bodies are usually present only in two to three-quarters of yolk sac tumors and are only seen in the papillary type. [14]

title: Yolk Sac Tumors -- History and Physical
content: Patients with yolk sac tumors have signs and symptoms depending on the location of the cancer. Testicular tumors have no specific symptoms except for a testicular mass. Children with testicular yolk sac tumors generally present with testicular masses; the mass is painless and solid. Metastasis is uncommon at presentation. It occurs in fewer than 1 in 10 cases. In adults, testicular yolk sac tumors are mixed with other germ cell components such as embryonal carcinoma, choriocarcinoma, teratoma, and seminoma. [15] Most patients with ovarian yolk sac tumors have symptoms of abdominal distention and sudden onset of pain at presentation. A pelvic mass may be palpable on physical examination. This tumor is characterized by rapid growth; the duration of symptoms in most patients is 7 days or less. [16] Other symptoms of ovarian cancer can include:

title: Yolk Sac Tumors -- History and Physical
content: Fatigue Upset stomach (dyspepsia) Back pain Pain during sex (dyspareunia) Constipation Changes in the period, such as more massive bleeding (menorrhagia) or irregular bleeding (metrorrhagia) Abdominal swelling with weight loss Metastasis develops quickly in ovarian yolk sac tumors and invades the structures around the ovaries. Metastasis can also spread through the lymph nodes. [17]

title: Yolk Sac Tumors -- Evaluation
content: Diagnosis of yolk sac tumors depends on history, physical examination, imaging studies, and blood chemistry. Yolk sac tumors were shown as an enhancing large solid cystic mass with intertumoral hemorrhage on CT and MR studies. [18] Immunohistochemical staining can support the diagnosis of yolk sac tumors, as almost all cases stain positively for alpha-fetoprotein (AFP). [19] Alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) is specific for yolk sac tumors but not sensitive (overall sensitivity as low as 60%) because it can be elevated in other cancers, such as hepatocellular carcinoma. [19]

title: Yolk Sac Tumors -- Evaluation
content: In mixed germ cell tumors with small foci of the yolk sac tumors, the biopsy findings may be negative for yolk sac tumors because yolk sac tumors are usually limited to small malignant foci within a larger tumor, staining positive for AFP confirms the presence of yolk sac tumors within other germ cell tumors, (eg, in teratoma the biopsy of cancer may reveal teratoma alone, whereas elevated AFP reveals that yolk sac tumor is also present.) [8]

title: Yolk Sac Tumors -- Evaluation
content: Alpha-fetoprotein can be measured in tumor tissue, serum, cerebrospinal fluid, urine, and amniotic fluid. [20] [21] When yolk sac tumor arises in a small focus only, it may be hard to detect AFP in immunohistochemical staining because staining for alpha-fetoprotein is unequable and often varies throughout the tissue; strong staining is not seen in every tumor; in this situation, yolk sac tumors may be marked with cytokeratin or glypican-3, cytokeratin is present in almost all cases, another immunostaining which is frequently positive in yolk sac tumors is placental alkaline phosphatase. [22] [23]

title: Yolk Sac Tumors -- Treatment / Management
content: Without any treatment, yolk sac tumors can be very dangerous and finally lead to death. The present-day treatment for yolk sac tumors is surgery and chemotherapy. Treatment with cisplatin, etoposide, and bleomycin has shown a good response in most patients. [24] [25] The treatment regimen of testicular yolk sac tumors depends on the stage of cancer and age of the patient at presentation; most children with yolk sac tumors present with stage 1 disease. Orchiectomy and chemotherapy +/- dissection of retroperitoneal lymph nodes, with careful post-orchiectomy measurement of serum AFP values, is indicated in most cases. Most pediatric patients with metastasis or recurrence can be successfully treated with a chemotherapy regimen. [26] Ovarian yolk sac tumors, specifically in post-menopausal patients, need more intensive treatment, and surgical resection of cancer with chemotherapy is indicated in the early stages of the disease. [27]

title: Yolk Sac Tumors -- Treatment / Management -- Stage 1
content: Stage 1 disease can be cured in almost all cases, and radical inguinal orchiectomy is performed in all patients.

title: Yolk Sac Tumors -- Treatment / Management -- Choices for Stage 1A
content: Careful observation (surveillance): this management includes visits every 2 months during the 1st year, with computed tomography scans every 4 to 6 months. Then, in the 2nd year, appointments are every 3 months, with computed tomography scans every 6 to 12 months. If cancer relapses, chemotherapy is indicated to treat the patient. Nerve-sparing retroperitoneal lymph node dissection (RPLND) Chemotherapy: giving the BEP regimen (bleomycin, etoposide, and cisplatin) for 1 cycle. Chemotherapy decreases the rate of relapse.

title: Yolk Sac Tumors -- Treatment / Management -- Stage 1S
content: Chemotherapy with 3 cycles of BEP or 4 cycles of EP (etoposide and cisplatin) is indicated if alpha-fetoprotein remains elevated after surgery, with no evidence of a mass on CT scan.

title: Yolk Sac Tumors -- Treatment / Management -- Stage 2
content: Surgery must be done 1st for all cases.

title: Yolk Sac Tumors -- Treatment / Management -- Stage 2A
content: Tumor marker values after surgery and the presence of retroperitoneal lymph node involvement determine the next step in management for those patients. Normal tumor marker levels: Retroperitoneal lymph node dissection (RPLND): If the lymph nodes contain cancer, then give 2 cycles of chemotherapy (BEP or EP). If no lymph nodes are involved, watch and monitor closely for signs of relapse. Chemotherapy: 4 cycles of EP (etoposide and cisplatin) or 3 cycles of BEP (bleomycin, etoposide, and cisplatin). High tumor markers after the surgery should be treated using chemotherapy (EP or BEP). The number of cycles is determined after the risk stratification (good, intermediate, or poor).

title: Yolk Sac Tumors -- Treatment / Management -- Stage 3
content: Patients with stage 3 disease should be treated with radical inguinal orchiectomy, followed by 3 to 4 cycles of the following chemotherapy regimens: EP 4 cycles BEP 3 or 4 cycles VIP (etoposide, ifosfamide, and cisplatin) 4 cycles High-dose chemotherapy and bone marrow transplant might be indicated in cancer resistance to usual dose chemotherapy.

title: Yolk Sac Tumors -- Differential Diagnosis
content: Clear Cell Carcinoma : stains positive for cytokeratin, cytokeratin 7, and epithelial membrane antigen, while stains negative for glypican-3 and alpha-fetoprotein. Yolk sac tumors stain negative for both cytokeratin 7 and epithelial membrane antigen. [28] [29]

title: Yolk Sac Tumors -- Staging
content: After the diagnosis of the yolk sac tumor has been established, many tests and evaluations should be done to decide if the cancer has spread to the lymph nodes or any parts of the body.

title: Yolk Sac Tumors -- Staging -- Testicular Tumors
content: Stage 0: The earliest stage of testicular cancer (it is also known as neoplasia in situ). Stage 4 does not apply to testicular cancer. The TNM system is the most popular system for staging testicular cancer, and the system is based on 4 elements: Tumor (T) : size and location of the tumor. Node (N) : lymph node involvement. Metastasis (M) : number and site of spread of the tumor. Serum tumor marker (S) : Are the serum tumor markers AFP, beta-hCG, and LDH elevated? If so, how high are they? Stage 1 : There is no evidence of metastasis or lymph node involvement. It is divided into 1A and 1B based on tumor size, and into 1S when tumor markers are elevated.

title: Yolk Sac Tumors -- Staging -- Testicular Tumors
content: Stage 2 : The cancer cells have spread to the lymph nodes, but there is no metastasis to other parts of the body. It is divided into 2A, 2B, and 2C based on the number and size of the involved lymph nodes. Stage 3 : Cancer has metastasized to other organs, and this stage is divided into 3A, 3B, and 3C depending on metastasis location and level of tumor markers.

title: Yolk Sac Tumors -- Staging -- Ovarian Cancer
content: The FIGO (International Federation of Gynecology and Obstetrics) and AJCC (American Joint Committee on Cancer) TNM staging systems are the same. They are the most widely used for staging ovarian cancers. Both of the systems contain 3 elements: Tumor (T) : size and location of the tumor. Node (N) : lymph node involvement. Metastasis (M) : number and site of spread of the tumor. Stage 1: the cancer is limited to the ovary (IA) or to both ovaries (IB).

title: Yolk Sac Tumors -- Staging -- Ovarian Cancer
content: Stage 2: cancer has spread to the pelvis (below pelvic brim) without lymph node involvement, and this stage is divided into 2A (spread to the uterus or the fallopian tubes) and 2B (other pelvic tissues). Stage 3: cancer has spread to the lymph nodes, and/or peritoneum outside the pelvis, and this stage is divided into 3A, 3B, and 3C, depending on metastasis location and size. Stage 4: cancer has spread to other tissues (distant metastasis excluding peritoneal metastasis), and this stage is divided into stages 4A (pleural effusion) and 4B (extra-abdominal metastasis). Staging systems are essential for determining the next step in patient management, as each stage has a unique treatment plan.

title: Yolk Sac Tumors -- Prognosis
content: Age at diagnosis is not a prognostic factor, but the degree of AFP elevation is a negative prognostic factor for yolk sac tumors. As with all malignancies, staging is vital for prognosis. Early-stage tumors fare better than late-stage malignancies.

title: Yolk Sac Tumors -- Complications
content: The complications of the yolk sac tumors can be related to the tumor itself or the treatment. Tumor mass effect complications depend on the location and the size of the mass; another tumor complication is metastasis; even if cancer has spread to other parts of the body, many patients might not have symptoms until very late stages. Treatment complications include chemotherapy side effects, operative complications, and postoperative complications.
